value.overview: The Ruddy Treerunner is a small, active ovenbird of the highlands of Costa Rica and western Panama. It is named for its reddish-brown plumage and habit of moving over trunks, branches, moss, and epiphyte-covered vegetation. Unlike true treecreepers, it belongs to the Furnariidae, or ovenbird family. Costa Rica holds much of the species’ northern range, making it a characteristic bird of humid mountain forests and high-elevation birding sites.
value.classification: The Ruddy Treerunner is a passerine in the ovenbird family, Furnariidae, and the genus Margarornis. Two subspecies are generally recognized, including the Costa Rican nominate form, Margarornis rubiginosus rubiginosus.
value.identification: This treerunner is about 15–17 cm long, with a compact body, short tail, and slightly curved bill. Adults are mainly warm rufous or reddish brown, with a paler eyebrow and eye-ring, a subdued reddish collar, and darker, patterned underparts. The sexes look alike. It is usually recognized more readily by its restless movements over mossy trunks and branches than by a single bold field mark. Its subdued colors help it blend into montane forest vegetation.
value.rangeHabitat: The Ruddy Treerunner has a restricted Central American range, occurring in Costa Rica and western Panama. In Costa Rica it is a resident of the mountain ranges, from the Cordillera de Guanacaste south through the Tilarán and Central Volcanic ranges to the Talamanca highlands. It inhabits humid montane evergreen forest, forest edges, and areas with abundant mosses, bromeliads, and other epiphytes, generally at elevations of about 1,200 m and above. It is regularly recorded at highland sites such as the Los Santos and Talamanca regions.
value.migrationStatus: It is considered a year-round resident in Costa Rica and throughout its range. Local movements may occur with changing conditions or elevation, but it is not known as a regular long-distance migrant.
value.breeding: In Costa Rica, documented nesting activity indicates a breeding period that includes March through May. The enclosed nest is an oval or globular mass of moss, epiphyte material, and fern pieces, attached to a trunk or the underside of a substantial branch and lined with plant fibers and fern scales. A tubular entrance opens from below. Studies at Monteverde and other Costa Rican highland sites found both adults participating in nest building and care; clutch size and incubation and fledging periods remain insufficiently known.
value.dietFeeding: The Ruddy Treerunner feeds mainly on small invertebrates found on or among bark, moss, lichens, bromeliads, and other epiphytes. It searches methodically while climbing along trunks and branches, probing crevices and inspecting vegetation. Its foraging behavior resembles that of a treecreeper, although it is unrelated to the true treecreepers. It may forage alone, in pairs, or as part of mixed-species flocks in montane forest.
value.behavior: This is an active, agile bird that frequently creeps along trunks and larger branches, often moving upward or sideways while clinging to uneven bark and epiphyte-covered surfaces. It is generally unobtrusive and can be difficult to detect until it gives a call or moves through nearby vegetation. In Costa Rica, observers often encounter it in humid cloud-forest habitats, where it may join mixed feeding flocks with other small highland birds.
